title: Dualizing an isogeny preserves its scheme-theoretic degree
statement:
Let $k$ be any field [def-weil-field], and let $A,B/k$ be abelian varieties [def-sc-abelian-variety] equipped with normalized dual Poincare data $(A^\vee,\mathcal P_A)$ and $(B^\vee,\mathcal P_B)$ [def-sfb-abelian-dual-poincare-datum]. Let $u:A\to B$ be an isogeny [def-sc-isogeny], that is, a surjective group-scheme homomorphism with finite scheme-theoretic kernel [def-sc-group-scheme]. Let $u^\vee:B^\vee\to A^\vee$ be the homomorphism classifying the rigidified family $(u\times1)^*\mathcal P_B$, so that $(1\times u^\vee)^*\mathcal P_A\simeq(u\times1)^*\mathcal P_B$ respecting the identity-axis rigidification; pullbacks are tensor inverse images [def-pc-module-pullback]. Then $u^\vee$ is an isogeny and
$$\deg(u^\vee)=\deg(u).$$
Here the degree is the order of the scheme-theoretic kernel, namely $\deg(v)=\dim_k\Gamma(\ker v,\mathcal O_{\ker v})$. No perfection of $k$, separability of $u$, or restriction on the characteristic is assumed.

source.place: I Theorem 9.1, printed p.41: the kernel of the dual isogeny is the Cartier dual of the kernel. Its coordinate algebra is the linear dual of the original finite-dimensional Hopf algebra, so its order is unchanged. This is the degree consequence, not an assertion about only geometric kernel points.

proof.text: Put $N=\ker u$ and $H=\Gamma(N,\mathcal O_N)$. The kernel is finite by hypothesis and commutative because $A$ is commutative. The isogeny-degree theorem makes $u$ finite flat; its surjectivity therefore makes it an fpqc cover. Abelian varieties are geometrically integral, so $H^0(A,\mathcal O_A)=k$. For every affine test $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$, flat coherent base change along the $k$-algebra $R$ gives $\Gamma(A\times S,\mathcal O)=R$ (every $k$-module is flat). These identifications restrict compatibly, hence hold for every scheme $S$ by gluing its affine opens. This verifies the universal global-functions hypothesis of pointed torsor descent, including when $S$ is nonreduced.

source.place: I Theorem 9.1, p.41: preparing finite-kernel descent; global functions are the proper-variety input

proof.text: The group-law formulas $(a,n)\mapsto(a,a+n)$ and $(a,a')\mapsto(a,a'-a)$ are inverse scheme maps $A\times N\simeq A\times_BA$: the equation $u(a)=u(a')$ says exactly $a'-a\in N$, functorially over every test algebra. Take $X=A$, $Y=B$, $G=N$, $q=u$, $x_0=0_A$, and $y_0=0_B$ in pointed torsor descent. For every $T$, it identifies characters $N_T\to\mathbf G_{m,T}$ with rigidified invertible modules $L$ on $B_T$ whose pullbacks to $A_T$ are trivial. Their normalized descent multipliers on $A_T\times_TN_T$ are exactly the characters, independent of the $A$ coordinate.

source.place: I Theorem 9.1, p.41: descent along the isogeny; Stacks 023T provides effective module descent

proof.text: Every line $L$ obtained in step 2 has algebraically trivial geometric fibres. Indeed, fix an algebraically closed geometric test field $\Omega$ and $b\in B(\Omega)$. The nonempty finite fibre $u_\Omega^{-1}(b)$ has an $\Omega$-point $a$: choose a maximal ideal in its nonzero finite-dimensional coordinate algebra; its residue field is finite over $\Omega$, hence is $\Omega$. Translation by $a$ on $A_\Omega$ commutes with the $N_\Omega$-action. The descent multiplier $\chi(n)$ is unchanged by that translation. Thus the identity between the two trivial lines upstairs respects descent, and full faithfulness of fpqc descent gives $t_b^*L_\Omega\simeq L_\Omega$. The homogeneous-line criterion now gives $L_\Omega\sim_{\rm alg}\mathcal O_{B_\Omega}$. This holds for every geometric fibre, exactly the condition in the normalized Poincare datum.

source.place: I Theorem 9.1 and Proposition 8.4(b), pp.35–36,41: the descended characters lie in Pic^0

proof.text: By the normalized Poincare universal property, a $T$-point of $\ker(u^\vee)$ is exactly a rigidified algebraically trivial family on $B_T$ whose pullback to $A_T$ is the rigidified trivial family: the defining equality for $u^\vee$ identifies its pullback family, and the zero map classifies the trivial family. Steps 2–3 show that these are precisely all the objects $K_u(T)$, hence precisely the characters of $N_T$. The identifications are natural in $T$ and take tensor products to multiplication. Cartier representability therefore identifies the group scheme $\ker(u^\vee)$ with $N^D=\operatorname{Spec}(H^*)$ (the natural maps are inverse by evaluating at the identity maps of the representing schemes). In particular this kernel is finite as a scheme.

source.place: I Theorem 9.1, p.41; Milne Algebraic Groups Theorem 11.12, pp.213–214

proof.text: Choose $n\geq1$ and $v:B\to A$ with $vu=[n]_A$ and $uv=[n]_B$ by the quasi-inverse lemma. The family $(v\times1)^*\mathcal P_A$ is fibrewise algebraically trivial (pullback carries a connected parameter family witnessing algebraic equivalence to such a family) and rigidified; it thus defines $v^\vee:A^\vee\to B^\vee$. Uniqueness in the Poincare universal property and composition of tensor inverse images give $(vu)^\vee=u^\vee v^\vee$. On every test scheme, multiplicativity of algebraically trivial lines, iterated along the diagonal, gives $[n]_A^*M\simeq M^{\otimes n}$. This can be normalized at zero: any discrepancy there is multiplication by a unit on the test scheme, which is removed by rescaling the isomorphism. The tensor law in the Poincare datum then gives $([n]_A)^\vee=[n]_{A^\vee}$. Thus $u^\vee v^\vee=[n]_{A^\vee}$.

source.place: I Remark 8.6, p.36, I §9 opening, p.41; I Proposition 8.4(c) and Corollary 8.5, pp.35–36

proof.text: Since $A^\vee$ is an abelian variety and $n\geq1$, multiplication $[n]_{A^\vee}$ is surjective. Its factorization $[n]_{A^\vee}=u^\vee v^\vee$ makes $u^\vee$ surjective on underlying points: any preimage under the composite gives a preimage under $u^\vee$. The hypothesis already makes $u^\vee$ a group-scheme homomorphism, and step 4 supplies its finite scheme-theoretic kernel. Hence it is an isogeny by definition.

source.place: I Theorem 9.1, p.41: surjectivity; I Remark 8.6 and multiplication isogenies

proof.text:
By step 4 and the definition of degree,
$$\deg(u^\vee)=\dim_k\Gamma(N^D,\mathcal O)=\dim_k H^*.$$
Choose a $k$-basis $h_1,\ldots,h_d$ of $H$; the coefficient functionals $h_1^*,\ldots,h_d^*$ form a basis of $H^*$, because $f=\sum_i f(h_i)h_i^*$ for every linear functional $f$. Therefore $\dim_kH^*=d=\dim_kH=\deg(u)$. This computation uses coordinate algebras, so it retains the length of nonreduced kernels.

source.place: I Theorem 9.1, p.41: degree consequence of Cartier duality; Milne Algebraic Groups §11c, p.212
